Sculpture. The art of creating three-dimensional form, either by subtractive methods—carving away material like stone or wood—or additive processes like modeling clay, assembling materials, or casting. As one of humanity's oldest arts, alongside painting and architecture, sculpture has served religious, commemorative, and aesthetic functions across all cultures.

Sculpture differs fundamentally from painting. Unlike painting's illusionistic window, sculpture occupies real space and invites the viewer's bodily presence and movement, creating an intimate physical dialogue between artwork and observer. Carving removes material to reveal form, with stone and wood as classical media. Modeling builds form from pliable material like clay. Casting reproduces an original in metal or plaster.

Marble became the canonical sculptural medium in antiquity, associated with durability, nobility, and idealized form. Quarries in Carrara, Italy supplied Renaissance masters. Greek sculpture evolved from rigid, frontal forms to contrapposto—a balanced weight-shift—naturalistic anatomy, and psychological expressiveness. These innovations became Renaissance touchstones. Michelangelo's sculptures, carved from single marble blocks, embodied Renaissance ideals of heroic human form and divine creation.

Gian Lorenzo Bernini revolutionized Baroque sculpture with theatrical drama, emotional intensity, and the manipulation of light on carved surfaces. In the modern era, Rodin introduced expressionist gesture and surface. Brancusi reduced form to pure abstraction. Constructivism employed industrial materials and geometric structure. Though sculpture shares exhibition space and institutional contexts with painting, it operates in fundamentally different spatial and temporal registers. It demands movement around and through it, a physical engagement distinct from the stationary viewing of a canvas.
